content: Sea-buckthorn, scientifically known as Hippophae L., belongs to the genus Hippophae within the family Elaeagnaceae. These are deciduous shrubs, and the name sea-buckthorn is hyphenated to distinguish it from buckthorns of the genus Rhamnus in the family Rhamnaceae. It is also referred to as sea buckthorn, seabuckthorn, sandthorn, or seaberry. Since 2005, there has been increasing recognition of sea-buckthorn berries in the United States, other developed countries, and the global functional food industry due to their exceptional nutrient content, antioxidant properties, and potential for consumer products, earning them the label of a novel superfruit. Description and Distribution There are six species and 12 subspecies of sea-buckthorn, native to a wide range of regions across Europe and Asia, including China, Mongolia, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Russia, Great Britain, France, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Norway. Approximately 5 million hectares of the world's sea-buckthorn resources are located in China, where the plant is utilized for soil and water conservation. These shrubs typically grow to a height of 5–6 meters, occasionally reaching up to 18 meters in Central Asia, and are commonly found in dry, sandy areas. They are highly tolerant of salt in both air and soil but require full sunlight for optimal growth and cannot thrive in shaded conditions near larger trees. The most widespread species is the common sea-buckthorn (Hippophae rhamnoides), which ranges from the Atlantic coasts of Europe to northwestern China. In Western Europe, it is primarily found along sea coasts, where salt spray inhibits competition from larger plants. In Central Asia, it is more prevalent in dry, semi-desert areas where other plants struggle to survive. In Central Europe and Asia, it also grows as a subalpine shrub above the tree line in mountainous regions and in other sunny areas such as riverbanks. The common sea-buckthorn has dense, stiff, and thorny branches, with pale silvery-green lanceolate leaves measuring 3–8 cm in length and less than 7 mm in width. The plant is dioecious, meaning male and female plants are separate. Male plants produce brownish flowers that release wind-distributed pollen. Names in Different Languages Sea-buckthorn is known by various names in different languages, such as Чацаргана (Mongolian), 沙棘 (Shaji, Chinese), Astelpaju (Estonian), Duindoorn (Dutch), Tyrni (Finnish), Argousier (French), Sanddorn (German), Olivello Spinoso (Italian), Облепиха (Oblepikha, Russian), Espino de Mar, Falso Espino, Espino Amarillo (Spanish), and Havtorn (Swedish and Danish). Berries and Leaves Female sea-buckthorn plants produce orange berries that are 6–9 mm in diameter, soft, juicy, and exceptionally rich in vitamin C, with an average content of 600 mg per 100 g and sometimes as high as 1500 mg per 100 g. Some varieties are also rich in vitamin A, vitamin E, and oils. These berries serve as an important winter food source for certain bird species, such as fieldfares. The leaves are consumed by the larvae of various Lepidoptera species, including the coastal race of the ash pug moth, brown-tail, the dun-bar, emperor moth, mottled umber, and Coleophora elaeagnisella. The species Hippophae salicifolia (willow-leaved sea-buckthorn) is restricted to the Himalayas, growing at high altitudes in dry valleys south of the range of H. rhamnoides. It differs in having broader (up to 10 mm wide), greener (less silvery) leaves and yellow berries. A wild variant of this species occurs at even higher altitudes in the alpine zone, where it grows as a low shrub, not exceeding 1 meter in height, with small leaves measuring 1–3 cm in length. Uses Harvesting and Landscaping Harvesting sea-buckthorn berries is challenging due to the dense thorns on the shrubs. A common method involves removing entire branches, which is destructive to the plant and reduces future yields. The harvested branches are frozen, allowing the berries to be easily shaken off. Branches are typically frozen to −32°C, slightly defrosted on the surface during berry removal, and then cleaned. Workers crush the berries to remove up to 95% of leaves and debris, which causes the berries to melt slightly during processing at ambient temperatures (around 20°C). The berries are later stored at −22°C. A more effective harvesting method involves using a berry-shaker, developed in Estonia, which minimizes damage to the branches. However, mechanical harvesting leaves up to 50% of the berries in the field and allows harvesting only once every two years, yielding about 25% of the potential crop. During the Cold War, Russian and East German horticulturists developed new varieties with improved nutritional value, larger berries, different ripening times, and branch forms that are easier to harvest. Over the past 20 years, experimental crops have been grown in the United States (Nevada and Arizona) and in western provinces of Canada. Sea-buckthorn is also a popular garden and landscaping shrub, valued for its colorful berry clusters that persist through winter. It is used as a vandal-proof barrier hedge and for stabilizing riverbanks and steep slopes. In northern climates, its ornamental qualities make it a valuable addition to landscapes. Florists use its branches for decorative purposes. The plant is the regional flora of the Finnish region of Satakunta. Nutrients, Potential Health Effects, and Cosmetics Sea-buckthorn berries are edible and highly nutritious but are very acidic and astringent, making them unpleasant to eat raw unless frosted to reduce astringency or mixed with sweeter substances like apple or grape juice. They can also be used to make pies, jams, lotions, and liquors. When pressed, sea-buckthorn juice separates into three layers: a thick orange cream on top, a middle layer rich in saturated and polyunsaturated fats, and sediment and juice at the bottom. The upper two layers are processed for skin creams and liniments, while the bottom layer is used for edible products. The berries contain high levels of antioxidants, which may have potential benefits for inflammatory disorders, cancer, and other diseases, although no specific health benefits have been conclusively proven in humans. The fruit is exceptionally rich in vitamin C, with an average content of 695 mg per 100 g, making it one of the most enriched plant sources of vitamin C. It also contains carotenoids, vitamin E, amino acids, dietary minerals, β-sitosterol, and polyphenolic acids. Sea-buckthorn is used as an ingredient in various commercially available cosmetic products and nutritional supplements. Its juice has a freezing point of −22°C, allowing it to remain liquid even in sub-zero temperatures. India’s Defence Research Development Organization has established a factory in Leh to produce a multi-vitamin herbal beverage based on sea-buckthorn juice for troops operating in extremely cold environments. Traditional Medicine Sea-buckthorn has been used in traditional medicine for centuries to treat various ailments. In China and other parts of Asia, it has been used to relieve cough, aid digestion, invigorate blood circulation, and alleviate pain. In Mongolia, extracts from sea-buckthorn branches and leaves are used to treat gastrointestinal distress in humans and animals. The bark and leaves are used to treat diarrhea, gastrointestinal and dermatological disorders, and as topical compresses for rheumatoid arthritis. The flowers may be used as a skin softener. The berries are added to medications for pulmonary, gastrointestinal, cardiac, blood, and metabolic disorders in Indian, Chinese, and Tibetan medicine. Components of the berries have shown potential anticancer activity. Fresh juice, syrup, and oils from the berries or seeds are used for colds, fever, exhaustion, stomach ulcers, cancer, and metabolic disorders. The oil, known as Chharma in some native languages, is used for liver diseases, inflammation, gastrointestinal disorders (including peptic ulcers and gastritis), eczema, canker sores, wounds, burns, frostbite, psoriasis, rosacea, lupus erythematosus, and chronic dermatoses. In ophthalmology, berry extracts have been used to treat keratitis, trachoma, eyelid injuries, and conjunctivitis. Organizations The International Center for Research and Training on Seabuckthorn (ICRTS) was established in 1988 through a collaboration between the China Research and Training Center on Seabuckthorn, the Seabuckthorn Office of the Yellow River Water Commission, and the Shaanxi Seabuckthorn Development Office. ICRTS published the research journal Hippophae from 1995 to 2000, but it does not appear to be active currently. In 2005, an international collaboration called EAN-Seabuck was initiated between European Union states, China, Russia, and New Independent States, funded by the European Commission, to promote sustainable crop and consumer product development from sea-buckthorn.
